question: What is the primary focus of a community diagnosis compared to an individual clinical diagnosis?

options.A: The specific disease pathology of a patient
options.B: The health status of a defined population
options.C: The genetic profile of a single family
options.D: The administrative budget of a local clinic

explanation: Community diagnosis shifts the clinical lens from a single person to a collective group or population within a shared setting. [learn more](GNS124_U3_T1#GNS124_U3_T1_h1)

question: Why is examining social determinants considered essential during a community diagnosis?

options.A: They provide accurate hospital admission statistics for doctors
options.B: They replace the need for physical examinations in the community
options.C: They determine the exact pharmacological dosage needed for patients
options.D: They reveal underlying environmental and economic causes of poor health

explanation: Social determinants like housing, income, and sanitation heavily influence the overall disease burden experienced by a population. [learn more](GNS124_U3_T1#GNS124_U3_T1_h1)

question: The establishment of a baseline during a community diagnosis is primarily used for what future purpose?

options.A: Determining hospital bed capacity for emergency admissions
options.B: Calculating individual patient drug dosages in the ward
options.C: Justifying staff salary increases to the ministry
options.D: Evaluating the success of subsequent health interventions

explanation: Baseline data gives public health workers a starting metric against which future improvements or changes can be measured accurately. [learn more](GNS124_U3_T1#GNS124_U3_T1_h2)

question: A local health team wants to distribute limited insecticide-treated nets across a region with high malaria rates. Which purpose of community diagnosis guides this action?
explanation: Allocating scarce public health materials based on identified community need is a direct application of resource allocation. [learn more](GNS124_U3_T1#GNS124_U3_T1_h2)

question: What characterizes a problem-oriented community diagnosis?

options.A: Focusing exclusively on hospital-based surgical procedures
options.B: Excluding environmental factors from the assessment entirely
options.C: Focusing on a single specific health issue or vulnerable group
options.D: Requiring years of exhaustive demographic data collection

explanation: A problem-oriented diagnosis zeroes in on a particular condition or crisis rather than attempting an exhaustive broad survey. [learn more](GNS124_U3_T1#GNS124_U3_T1_h3)

question: When would a comprehensive community diagnosis be less practical than a problem-oriented one?

options.A: When establishing long-term health policies for a new district
options.B: During an acute disease outbreak requiring immediate containment
options.C: When funding and personnel are abundant for a five-year study
options.D: When baseline demographic data is completely missing

explanation: Comprehensive assessments take too long when quick, targeted action is mandatory to stop an active epidemic. [learn more](GNS124_U3_T1#GNS124_U3_T1_h3)

question: What is the very first step typically undertaken when beginning a community diagnosis process?
explanation: Entering a community properly and gaining approval from local leaders must happen before any data collection can begin. [learn more](GNS124_U3_T1#GNS124_U3_T1_h4)

question: Why must priority setting occur before drafting an action plan in community health?

options.A: Resources are limited, forcing teams to address the most urgent needs first
options.B: Data analysis cannot be finished without a finalized action plan
options.C: Community members refuse to talk to nurses who prioritize minor issues
options.D: Government regulations forbid treating more than one disease at a time

explanation: Because health needs always outstrip available resources, nurses must prioritize which problems to tackle first. [learn more](GNS124_U3_T1#GNS124_U3_T1_h4)

question: Which activity represents the collection of primary data during a community diagnosis?

options.A: Reviewing disease notification registers at the ministry
options.B: Analyzing census publications from ten years ago
options.C: Reading past mortality statistics from a library archive
options.D: Conducting household interviews and focus group discussions

explanation: Primary data is gathered directly from the population under study through active interaction and observation. [learn more](GNS124_U3_T1#GNS124_U3_T1_h5)

question: What is the main value of performing a windshield survey?

options.A: It automatically cures chronic malnutrition in children
options.B: It replaces the need for community leaders to give permission
options.C: It generates accurate demographic census numbers for the entire country
options.D: It provides direct visual observation of environmental and living conditions

explanation: A windshield survey allows nurses to observe housing quality, drainage, waste disposal, and other visible health determinants firsthand. [learn more](GNS124_U3_T1#GNS124_U3_T1_h5)

question: How are identified health problems typically validated after data analysis is complete?

options.A: By assuming statistical models are always flawless without review
options.B: By submitting the raw numbers exclusively to international donors
options.C: By immediately destroying all survey questionnaires to protect privacy
options.D: By presenting findings back to community stakeholders for confirmation

explanation: Sharing analyzed data with the community ensures the identified problems genuinely match local experiences and perceptions. [learn more](GNS124_U3_T1#GNS124_U3_T1_h6)

question: A nurse discovers that a rural community has a maternal mortality ratio three times higher than the national average. What does this comparison indicate?

options.A: A significant community health problem requiring targeted intervention
options.B: That primary data collection is completely unnecessary
options.C: That national health standards no longer apply to rural areas
options.D: An error in data collection that should be ignored

explanation: Comparing local rates to national benchmarks helps isolate specific health deficits that demand urgent programmatic focus. [learn more](GNS124_U3_T1#GNS124_U3_T1_h6)

question: Which criterion used in priority setting refers to the number of people affected by a health condition?
explanation: Magnitude measures the sheer scale or prevalence of a health problem within the population. [learn more](GNS124_U3_T1#GNS124_U3_T1_h7)

question: Why is 'feasibility' an essential factor when deciding which health problem to address first?

options.A: It guarantees that the community will never experience another disease
options.B: It ensures the health team has the resources and capability to solve the issue
options.C: It eliminates the need for any community participation during implementation
options.D: It measures how severely a disease impacts individual organ systems

explanation: Feasibility assesses whether an intervention is actually achievable given existing financial, logistical, and technical constraints. [learn more](GNS124_U3_T1#GNS124_U3_T1_h7)

question: What primary role does the public health nurse assume when engaging community stakeholders?
explanation: Nurses facilitate collaboration, guiding the community to identify solutions rather than imposing outside rules. [learn more](GNS124_U3_T1#GNS124_U3_T1_h8)

question: What is the main benefit of involving traditional and religious leaders in community health interventions?

options.A: They provide specialized surgical training for junior nursing staff
options.B: They replace the need for conducting formal household surveys
options.C: They help bridge cultural gaps and improve local acceptance of health programs
options.D: They audit the financial expenditures of the national government

explanation: Trusted community leaders hold immense influence over local attitudes, making their endorsement vital for participation. [learn more](GNS124_U3_T1#GNS124_U3_T1_h8)

question: What is the difference between monitoring and evaluation?

options.A: Monitoring happens only after a project ends, while evaluation occurs daily
options.B: Monitoring tracks activities during implementation, while evaluation assesses ultimate impact
options.C: Monitoring is done by the community, while evaluation is done by foreign experts
options.D: Monitoring focuses on financial budgeting, while evaluation focuses on surgery

explanation: Monitoring is continuous tracking during the project, whereas evaluation measures overall results and outcomes at or after completion. [learn more](GNS124_U3_T1#GNS124_U3_T1_h9)

question: When is formative evaluation most effectively carried out?

options.A: During the ongoing implementation of the intervention to allow adjustments
options.B: Years after the health program has been completely terminated
options.C: Before any community entry or data collection has even started
options.D: Exclusively during the initial priority-setting committee meeting

explanation: Formative evaluation provides feedback while the project is running so nurses can fix operational flaws immediately. [learn more](GNS124_U3_T1#GNS124_U3_T1_h9)
